I too am a private person but encourage all women to break through their reservations and talk to their doctors and physicians. We must also banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who were diagnosed in their 20s, an age when most women are graduating from college and just starting their lives as full adults.  Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk » . Women in their 20s and 30s should have a clinical breast exam by a health professional at least once every three years and women 40 and older should have an exam every year. I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, myself, my children and future generations of women, so one day we will not have to be afraid of breast cancer. I began my fight by learning important first steps in breast cancer detection, and will not end my fight until every woman can stand together saying we are breast cancer free. More than anything else, I have faith -- faith we will find a cure. I saw this commitment in the faces of the women in Washington -- in the faces of the women walking and the women and men who stood on the sidelines encouraging the 3,500 participants to the finish line. I was cheering right along with them, screaming for action to find a cure.  Avon's next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

Editor’s Note: Reese Witherspoon, an Academy Award-winning actress, serves as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation and works with Avon Products as its global ambassador. She says she hopes to dispel the false belief that breast cancer does not threaten young women.

(CNN) — In the United States, a woman receives a breast cancer diagnosis every three minutes. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that number deeply frightening. I was never unaware of the dangers of breast cancer, but hearing that statistic made the reality of it unmistakably clear.

Women I care about have faced this illness and have gone on to become fighters in the broader battle against it. Still, when I heard the phrase “every three minutes,” I felt exposed and afraid, because it reminded me that no one is immune. The only way I could calm that fear was to do something. I knew I had to learn more about the disease and help inform others as well.

In my role as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation, I had valuable support available to me. I was connected to an entire organization committed to helping women and spreading awareness. So I began by asking, “What do I need to understand?”

That desire to learn led me to the most crucial truth about breast cancer: finding it early can save lives. The Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade reports that when breast cancer is discovered before it has moved to other areas of the body, the five-year survival rate is 97 percent.

In its earliest stages, breast cancer often produces no signs at all. That is why women should examine themselves regularly and reach out to their doctors if they notice even the slightest change.

Talking about breast cancer and breast health can, of course, feel very personal. I am a private person too, but I urge women to move past their hesitation and speak with their doctors and medical professionals.

We also have to eliminate the misconception that breast cancer is not a concern for younger women. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who had been diagnosed while still in their 20s, a time when many women are finishing college and beginning adult life.

Women in their 20s and 30s should receive a clinical breast exam from a health care professional at least once every three years. Women who are 40 or older should have one every year.

I feel strongly committed to fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, for myself, for my children, and for generations of women still to come, with the hope that one day breast cancer will no longer be something we fear.

My own fight began with learning the basic first steps in breast cancer detection, and I will not stop until every woman can stand together and say that we are free from breast cancer.

Above all, I have faith — faith that a cure will be found. I saw that same dedication on the faces of the women in Washington: the women who walked, and the women and men along the route who encouraged the 3,500 participants all the way to the finish line. I was cheering with them, calling for action to help find a cure.

Avon’s next walk is scheduled to take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

## Opinion: Breast cancer awareness is personal. Early detection can save lives.

Breast cancer is one of those diagnoses that seems to touch nearly every family. A mother. A sister. A friend. A colleague. Sometimes the strongest women we know are the ones quietly navigating doctors’ appointments, biopsies, chemotherapy, radiation, surgery and recovery while still trying to keep their lives—and the lives of the people they love—moving forward.

That is why breast cancer awareness can’t be limited to a ribbon, a month or a slogan. Awareness has to lead to action: knowing your risk, understanding your body, talking to your doctor and getting screened.

According to the American Cancer Society, breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the United States after skin cancer. In 2024, an estimated more than 310,000 new cases of invasive breast cancer were expected to be diagnosed among women in the US. Globally, the World Health Organization reports that breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women, with millions of families affected around the world.

Those numbers are sobering. But there is also hope. When breast cancer is found early, before it has spread, the five-year relative survival rate is about 99%, according to the American Cancer Society. That statistic is not just a number—it is a reminder that early detection matters.

For many women, mammograms are a critical tool. The guidance on when to begin screening can vary depending on age, family history, genetics and personal risk factors, so every woman should have a conversation with her health care provider about what is right for her. Some women may need to start screening earlier or consider additional imaging. Others may need help simply getting access to care.

And that is where advocacy becomes essential.

Through work with organizations such as the Avon Foundation, the mission has long been clear: expand access to breast cancer education, screening and care, especially for underserved women who may face barriers because of cost, geography, language, insurance status or lack of information. The fight against breast cancer is not only a medical issue; it is also an equity issue.

No woman should miss a potentially life-saving screening because she cannot afford it. No family should be left without support because they live in the wrong ZIP code. No patient should feel alone because resources are difficult to find or conversations about cancer are surrounded by fear.

Events such as the Avon Walk for Breast Cancer have helped bring thousands of people together—survivors, families, caregivers, doctors, volunteers and advocates—to raise awareness and funding for research, education, screening and support services. The power of those walks is not only in the miles covered. It is in the message they send: We show up for one another.

Breast cancer awareness is also about listening. Listening to patients who say something feels different. Listening to communities that have been underserved. Listening to doctors and researchers who remind us that early detection and better treatments save lives. Listening to survivors who tell us that support can make an unbearable moment feel a little less lonely.

So this month—and every month—make the appointment. Ask about your risk. Encourage someone you love to get screened. Learn your family history if you can. Support organizations working to bring care to women who need it most. And if you are able, participate in events like the Avon Walk or contribute to groups funding breast cancer research and patient support.

A ribbon can be a symbol of hope. But action is what turns hope into change.

## Young Women, Your Health Deserves Your Attention

Let’s talk about something that isn’t always easy to bring up at brunch, in a group chat, or while juggling school, work, family, and everything else life throws at us: breast health.

For many young women, breast cancer can feel like something far away—something that happens “later” or to someone else. But the truth is, while breast cancer is more common as women get older, younger women can and do get diagnosed. And because it’s not always expected, symptoms may be overlooked or dismissed.

That’s why taking your health seriously is not about fear. It’s about confidence. It’s about knowing your body, trusting yourself, and making sure you get the care you deserve.

### Know What’s Normal for You

Every woman’s body is different. Your breasts may change throughout your menstrual cycle, with pregnancy, while breastfeeding, or due to hormones and aging. The important thing is learning what feels normal for *you*.

If you notice a new lump, swelling, skin dimpling, nipple discharge, persistent pain, redness, or any change that feels unusual, don’t ignore it. Don’t talk yourself out of calling the doctor because you’re “too young” or “probably fine.”

You are allowed to ask questions. You are allowed to insist on being checked. You are allowed to take up space in a doctor’s office.

### Regular Exams Matter

Routine checkups are one of the most powerful tools we have. A healthcare provider can help you understand your personal risk, including family history, genetic factors, and when you may need screenings like clinical breast exams, mammograms, or other imaging.

If breast cancer runs in your family—especially if a close relative was diagnosed at a young age—bring that up with your doctor. You may need a different screening plan than someone at average risk.

And if you don’t know your family history, that’s okay too. Your doctor can still help you make informed decisions.

### Don’t Let Busy Become an Excuse

Young women are often carrying so much. Careers, classes, relationships, caregiving, friendships, finances—the list never ends. It’s easy to put your own health at the bottom of the pile.

But your health is not a luxury. It is the foundation that allows you to show up for your dreams, your people, and yourself.

Make the appointment. Put it on the calendar. Bring a friend if you’re nervous. Set a reminder. Ask questions. Follow up.

That little act of self-care could make all the difference.

### Early Detection Can Save Lives

When breast cancer is found earlier, treatment is often more effective. That’s why awareness, regular doctor visits, and timely evaluation of symptoms matter so much.

This doesn’t mean living in anxiety. It means living informed. It means paying attention. It means treating your body like something precious—because it is.

### A Message to Young Women

Please don’t wait until something feels “serious enough.” Please don’t dismiss your concerns because you’re young. Please don’t be embarrassed to talk about your breasts, your body, or your fears.

You deserve care. You deserve answers. You deserve a doctor who listens.

So check in with yourself. Schedule that appointment. Encourage your friends to do the same. Talk openly. Share information. Support one another.

Because taking breast health seriously is not just about preventing illness—it’s about honoring your life, your future, and the woman you are becoming.

## We Can’t Stop Until Breast Cancer Is Curable

By an Avon Foundation honorary chair and breast cancer advocate

Breast cancer is one of those issues that can feel both deeply personal and overwhelmingly vast. Nearly everyone knows someone — a mother, sister, daughter, friend, colleague or neighbor — whose life has been changed by this disease. For too many families, breast cancer is not an abstract health statistic. It is a diagnosis that arrives like a thunderclap and reshapes everything that comes after.

And yet, there is reason for hope.

Over the past several decades, advances in screening, treatment and awareness have helped more women survive breast cancer than ever before. When breast cancer is found early and remains localized, the five-year relative survival rate is about 99%, according to the American Cancer Society. That number represents extraordinary progress — and it reminds us why access to mammograms, education and timely care matters so much.

But hope should never make us complacent.

Breast cancer remains one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers among women in the United States. Risk increases with age, and factors such as family history, inherited genetic mutations, breast density, reproductive history, alcohol use and lifestyle can all play a role. But the painful truth is that many women diagnosed with breast cancer have no obvious risk factors at all. That is why awareness must be paired with action — and why every woman deserves access to accurate information, preventive care and screening.

The survival numbers also tell another story. If breast cancer spreads to distant parts of the body, the five-year survival rate drops dramatically. For people living with metastatic breast cancer, progress has not come fast enough. Their courage should compel us to do more — to fund more research, improve treatments, expand clinical trial access and keep pushing toward the cure that patients and families urgently need.

We also have to confront the inequities that still define too many breast cancer outcomes. In the United States, Black women are more likely to die from breast cancer than white women, even though incidence rates are similar. That disparity is not inevitable. It reflects gaps in access, diagnosis, treatment, trust, transportation, insurance coverage and the quality of care patients receive. Saving lives means closing those gaps.

As someone committed to this cause, I believe awareness is only the beginning. Wearing pink, sharing stories and encouraging screening are important — but we must match compassion with investment. We need better science, better access and better support for patients at every stage of the journey.

That means funding researchers who are searching for more effective therapies. It means supporting community programs that help women get screened, especially in underserved areas. It means making sure patients have the resources to navigate treatment without being crushed financially or emotionally. And it means listening to survivors and those living with metastatic disease, because their experiences should shape the future of care.

Breast cancer has taken too much from too many people. But the progress we have made proves that change is possible. Survival rates can improve. Treatments can become more precise. Early detection can save lives. And one day, with enough urgency and commitment, a cure can be within reach.

Until then, we cannot look away. We cannot assume someone else will solve it. We owe it to every woman facing a diagnosis today — and every family hoping they never hear those words tomorrow — to keep fighting.

Because awareness matters. Survival matters. Equity matters.

And finding a cure matters most of all.

**What We Owe Ourselves—and the Women We Love: A Call for Breast Cancer Awareness**

As women, we spend so much of our lives taking care of other people.

We remember the pediatrician appointments, the school forms, the birthdays, the groceries, the phone calls to check in on our parents, the late-night conversations with friends who need us. We show up for our families, our communities, our work, and our dreams.

But too often, we put our own health at the bottom of the list.

Breast cancer reminds us why we can’t afford to do that.

As a mother, I think about the example we set for our children—not only in what we say, but in what we do. When we make preventive care a priority, when we schedule our screenings, when we ask questions and advocate for ourselves, we teach our daughters and sons that health is not something to postpone. It is something to protect.

As a daughter, I think about the women who raised us, guided us, and shaped us. Many of them grew up in a time when breast cancer was whispered about, feared, or hidden. Today, we know better. We know that conversation can save lives. We know that early detection matters. And we know that no woman should feel ashamed or alone when facing a diagnosis.

As an actress, I’ve had the privilege of telling women’s stories—stories of courage, vulnerability, resilience, humor, and hope. But some of the most powerful stories are not written for the screen. They happen in doctors’ offices, at kitchen tables, in support groups, and in quiet moments when a woman decides to make the appointment she has been putting off.

And as someone who has worked with Avon’s global efforts to raise awareness around breast cancer, I’ve seen how far-reaching this issue is. Breast cancer touches women in every community, every country, every background, and every stage of life. It affects mothers, sisters, daughters, friends, coworkers, and neighbors. It affects families emotionally, physically, and financially. That is why awareness is not just a campaign. It is a responsibility.

Breast cancer prevention begins with knowledge. While not every case can be prevented, there are steps that can help lower risk: maintaining a healthy lifestyle, staying physically active, limiting alcohol, avoiding tobacco, and talking with a healthcare provider about personal risk factors, including family history and genetics.

Early detection is just as critical. Regular mammograms, clinical breast exams, and knowing what is normal for your own body can make an enormous difference. A lump is not the only sign of breast cancer. Changes in breast size or shape, skin dimpling, nipple discharge, redness, swelling, or persistent pain should be discussed with a medical professional.

The message is simple: don’t wait.

Don’t wait because you are busy.  
Don’t wait because you are scared.  
Don’t wait because you think it can’t happen to you.  
Don’t wait because taking care of everyone else feels more urgent.

Your health is urgent, too.

Too many women face barriers to screening and care—cost, lack of insurance, transportation, language, geography, or fear. Awareness must be paired with action. That means supporting community clinics, mobile screening programs, patient navigation services, research, education, and policies that make breast cancer care more affordable and accessible.

No woman should miss a lifesaving screening because of her ZIP code or bank account.

Breast cancer awareness is often symbolized by a pink ribbon, but the real power of that ribbon is what it asks of us: to talk, to listen, to act, and to care. It asks us to call a friend and say, “Have you scheduled your mammogram?” It asks us to share information with our mothers and daughters. It asks us to support those in treatment not only with words, but with meals, rides, childcare, and compassion.

Most of all, it asks us to believe that women’s lives are worth prioritizing.

So today, make the appointment. Encourage someone you love to make theirs. Learn your family history. Know your body. Ask questions. Seek care. Offer support.

Because breast cancer is not just a medical issue. It is a family issue. A community issue. A women’s health issue. A human issue.

And when we take it seriously—when we choose prevention, early detection, access, and awareness—we give more women the chance to keep living their stories.

Breast cancer is a disease that touches families, friendships, workplaces, and communities. For too many women, the challenge is not only the diagnosis itself, but also the fear, uncertainty, and barriers to getting the care they need. That is why the Avon Breast Cancer Crusade has meant so much to me.

Through the Avon Breast Cancer Crusade, Avon has helped raise awareness and funding for breast cancer education, screening, treatment access, and research. The mission is simple but urgent: make sure more women have the information, support, and medical resources they need—especially those who might otherwise go without care.

One of the most powerful ways people can get involved is through the Avon Walk for Breast Cancer. The Walk brings together survivors, families, friends, advocates, and supporters who are united by a shared goal: to help end breast cancer and support those living with it now.

This upcoming Avon Walk is more than a fundraising event. It is a public show of strength and solidarity. Every step represents someone’s mother, sister, daughter, friend, or colleague. Every dollar raised helps expand the reach of breast cancer programs and supports the work being done to improve outcomes for women and families.

I’ve always believed that when women come together, we can create extraordinary change. The Avon Walk is a reminder that advocacy does not have to be abstract—it can be a step, a donation, a conversation, a mammogram appointment made, or a hand held during treatment.

I encourage everyone who can to join the Walk, support a participant, or learn more about the Avon Breast Cancer Crusade. Breast cancer is a deeply personal fight for millions, but no one should have to face it alone. Together, we can help bring hope, resources, and real progress to the people who need them most.
